tier_statements.essential: Built on attachment theory, a validated five-factor measure and Goleman's EQ framework. The archetype instrument itself is developmental: the questions are ours, and their properties are still being established.
tier_statements.closeness: The two dimensions come from a large and well-replicated research tradition. The questions are ours, written for this instrument, and their properties are still being established.
tier_statements.eq: A Goleman four-domain emotional intelligence read.
tier_statements.everyday: Forced-choice pairs about ordinary life, so self-description can't do the answering. Ours, and the newest thing here: the option pairs have not yet been tested for whether one sounds more flattering than the other, so this instrument contributes to a reading and never anchors one alone.

promise_opening: We cannot find you love. Nobody can. Every promise we make is about you, because that’s the only person we can honestly make one about.

promises.title: Every promise is about you.
promises.body: We cannot find you love. Nobody can. No output here will ever predict another person’s behaviour, promise a meeting, or put a date on anything. We make promises about the one person we can honestly make them about: you.

promises.title: Free to start.
promises.body: Free. No card required. And not a trial — nothing expires, nothing converts, nothing quietly becomes a subscription while you’re not looking. An account is needed to begin: a name, an email, and where you are right now. That is the whole of it, and it exists so the report can be written for you and handed back when you return.

promises.title: It ends.
promises.body: Anything paid runs three months, then it stops. No renewal, nothing to cancel. The practice is finite and completable — it is designed to be finished and left, not to retain you.

promises.title: A ceiling, in writing.
promises.body: There is a maximum price here — one ceiling for the whole practice, and it will be published on this page before anything is purchasable. That is a standing public commitment, not a price point: once the figure is up, raising it would be a reputational event, and we know it.

promises.title: No urgency.
promises.body: No countdowns, no scarcity, no places-are-limited, no time-limited pricing. A decision made under pressure isn’t a decision — it’s a capture. Everything here will still be here tomorrow.

promises.title: No upsell.
promises.body: No inner circle, no mastermind, no next level. And nobody here will phone you.

promises.title: No number we cannot justify.
promises.body: No compatibility percentages. No banded scores before norms exist to justify them. Every instrument publishes its evidence tier in full — including the word “developmental” where it applies to our own.

refusals: A clinical label — of you, or of anyone you describe
A verdict on anyone who hasn’t taken the assessment
refusals_intro: Ten classes of claim that are banned outright — in our copy, in anything machine-written, and in every partner’s promotion. Any output containing one of these is rejected, whoever wrote it.
promise_close: Two more, behind the scenes. We never ask who you’re assessing, and there is no profile and no matching — the only person described here is you. Your data is never sold, never shared, and never used to train any model — contractually, not aspirationally. And anything machine-written is disclosed, plainly, where it appears.
It’s a self-reflection instrument, not a clinical tool. It informs conversations; it does not replace professionals.

safety.headline: If you’re ever afraid of someone, that isn’t a pattern to work on.
paragraphs: Everything on this site is about patterns — noticing them, measuring them, deciding what to do with them. One category is exempt from all of that, and it matters that we say so plainly.

Control, coercion, monitoring, isolation, and fear of a specific person are not flags to weigh, not material for reflection, and not something any instrument here should be used on. They are a different category with a different answer, and the answer is support from people whose job this is.
safety.floor: Fear of a specific person is always information — and never something to talk yourself out of.
safety.outside_uk: Outside the UK, the equivalent services in your country are the right first step — most countries run a national domestic abuse line and a crisis line. Nothing on this site is a substitute for them, and nothing you read here should ever be a reason to stay somewhere you’re afraid.
safety.exit_link: If you’re afraid of someone, start here

flag_check.label: Flag Check · A reflection, not a measure
flag_check.subtitle: It reads you, not them.
flag_check.safety_split: Control, coercion, monitoring, isolation, and fear of a specific person are not material for reflection. If that’s where you are, this isn’t the page —
flag_check.safety_split_lead: One category is exempt from everything below.
intro_paragraphs: Eight situations people recognise. Not one of them asks you to rate, diagnose or describe another person — every question is about what you noticed, when, and what you did with it.

There's no score at the end, no band, no grade. What you get back is a reflection of your own noticing pattern, and a framework for what to do with an observation that isn't “leave” and isn't “let it go”.
intro_meta: 9 questions · about 3 minutes · no account needed
Answer from your own history, across relationships — not about any one person.
flag_check.prompt: Have you been somewhere like this?
flag_check.disclosure: A reflection, not a measure. No score was produced, nothing was graded, and nothing here is a diagnosis — these questions never asked about anyone but you.
flag_check.safety_yes_lead: You said part of this is about someone you’re afraid of. Then set the reflection aside — it isn’t the point.
flag_check.safety_yes_body: Fear of a specific person is always information — and never something to talk yourself out of. Nothing on this page is a reason to stay anywhere you’re afraid, and working on your “noticing” is not the assignment. The right next step is people whose job this is:
flag_check.safety_unsure_body: You weren’t sure whether some of this is about someone you’re afraid of. That uncertainty deserves respect rather than analysis — if any part of you is checking, the checking itself is worth taking seriously. Fear of a specific person is always information.
flag_check.graduated_note: One category is exempt from graduation: anything involving fear, control or coercion is not a yellow flag to explore. It has a different answer, and it’s on
stages: is this a pattern or an incident? does it recur?
raise it, if it's worth raising
flag_check.cta_body: The thing underneath the noticing — what you’re drawn to, what you excuse, and the gap between who you are and who you say you want — is measurable. That’s the Essential Mirror.

reprice.title: You see it early, and you let it count.
reprice.body: On your own account, when something has felt off you've tended to notice it at the time and let it change how you read what came next. That's a noticing pattern that works. The risk for you isn't blindness — it's the opposite: letting a single observation become a verdict before it's a pattern. One instance is human; repetition is information.
reprice.position: Your work mostly lives at Reflect: pattern or incident? Does it recur? You can afford to ask, because you don’t lose the observation by waiting.

explain.title: You see it early — and find a reason it’s fine.
explain.body: On your own account, the noticing itself works: things registered at the time. What happened next is the interesting part — the observation got explained, softened, or priced back down. That isn't foolishness; it's what investment does. Seeing clearly and letting it count are different skills, and the second one is buildable.
explain.position: Your work sits between Notice and Reflect: keeping the observation alive long enough to check whether it repeats. Not as a verdict — as a record. An observation written down is much harder to renegotiate.

late.title: It tends to arrive in hindsight.
late.body: On your own account, the pattern mostly became visible afterwards, looking back. Two things are true about that. Slow-arriving things are genuinely hard to see from inside — they arrive gradually, dressed as something good, while you're invested. And hindsight isn't failure; it's data about where your attention wasn't pointed.
late.position: Your work starts at Notice: logging what you observe in real time, without needing it to mean anything yet. Noticing without conclusion is the whole first stage — the rest can wait.

mixed.title: Your noticing changes with the situation.
mixed.body: No single pattern dominated your answers — by your own account, sometimes things counted early, sometimes they got explained away or only arrived in hindsight. That's common, and it usually means the noticing depends on how invested you are. Which is itself worth knowing.
mixed.position: Your work spans Notice and Reflect: observe in real time, then check honestly whether the observation survives your own investment.

insufficient.title: Not much to reflect back — and that’s an honest result.
insufficient.body: Most of your answers said these situations haven't come up, or aren't recallable. We won't invent a pattern out of thin data — that would be a horoscope, and you were promised otherwise. If more of your history surfaces later, this takes three minutes to do again.
insufficient.position: If and when something does register, the framework below is the shape of what to do with it — starting with Notice: observation without conclusion.

data_claim: We never ask who you’re assessing. No profile, no matching, no browsing other people, no verdict on anyone who hasn’t taken the assessment. Your answers are never sold, never shared, and never used to train any model — contractually, not aspirationally.
account_claim: Three fields — a name, an email, and where you are right now. No card, no social login, and nothing emailed at you: your results appear on screen and stay retrievable by logging back in.
disclaimer: It’s a self-reflection instrument, not a clinical tool. It informs conversations; it does not replace professionals.
honest_line: It can’t find you anyone. Nothing can.

position._note: Approved replacement for the 'commonness' block (norms pause, B3). Every population statement is gone rather than caveated: a note saying the bands rest on nothing, printed beside a sentence comparing the reader to other people, is an admission of doing it anyway. `no_grade` was renamed `no_comparison` because it is now doing the opposite of its old job. Restore population copy only when a reference sample exists and its n and composition are published.
position.heading: Where each factor sits in your own profile
position.caveat_heading: What these rows do and don't say
position.caveat_body: Each row shows which way you lean, and marks the three that sit furthest from your own middle. What they do not show is how you compare with anybody else. We have not yet established the reference sample that would make a comparison honest, so we are not making one. When we have, it will be published here before it appears in a reading.
position.no_comparison: There is no good end and no bad end. Every line here compares you with you.
position.globals_explainer: These five are derived, not measured: each is a weighted sum of the primary factors, clipped to fit a 1–10 scale. That's why they show a position and their equation rather than a number about you on its own.
position.loudest_heading: The three furthest from your own middle
position.loudest_meaning: Traits at this distance are the ones doing the selecting — what you notice first in somebody, and what you are most likely to over-weight.
position.loudest_partial_one: One factor sits far enough from your own middle to name. A flatter profile means no single trait is doing most of the selecting, which is worth knowing in itself.
position.loudest_partial: {count} of your factors sit far enough from your own middle to name. A flatter profile means no single trait is doing most of the selecting, which is worth knowing in itself.
position.loudest_none: None of your factors sits far enough from your own middle to name one confidently. That is a real result rather than a missing one.

junction._note: C1 · the Junction Check closing line, fixed and hash-locked. The instrument produces no score, no band and no statement about a second person; this is the sentence that says what it is for.
junction.closing_lead: A junction passed is passed. You cannot re-route from the middle of a section.
junction.closing_body: None of this tells you who to be with. It is six things worth saying out loud early, when asking still costs a fortnight of mild awkwardness rather than four years.

landing._note: B4/B5 · the public-page claims. Locked because these are the strings that put the product in breach of its own promise 07 when they drift: promise 07 says no banded scores before norms exist to justify them, and docs/B3_NORMS_PROVENANCE.md establishes that no reference sample is documented. 'calibrated norms', 'published norms', 'population middle' and 'norm bands' are banned in reader-facing copy by tests/test_copy_lint.py while reliability_1_0_0.json has placeholder=true.
landing.hero_sub: No card. An email, so the reading is still here when you come back. No profiles, and nobody else involved.
landing.tiers_line: Two are established instruments built on published research. Three are ours, built on established research and still being established — we label them that way on every page they appear.
landing.banding_note: Both established instruments report positions rather than bands. The reference sample that would justify banding — the Personality Mirror's stens and the EI Mirror's cut-offs alike — is not yet established, and promise 07 says we won't band before it is. An evidence tier describes where an instrument came from, not its banding.
landing.fixed_order: There's one door in, and it's the Essential Mirror. The rest follow in a fixed order, because each one changes how you read the one before it — the Everyday Mirror is the only instrument here that can contradict what you said about yourself, and it comes second for exactly that reason.
landing.it_ends_body: Anything paid runs three months and then stops. No renewal, nothing to cancel, nothing that quietly becomes a subscription while you are not looking. The practice is finite and completable — built to be finished and left rather than to keep you.
landing.it_ends_tail: Which is also why there is no inner circle, no next level, and nobody here who will phone you.
landing.free_tier_body: Your Delta, your pattern, and the full description. No card.
landing.paid_prose: Two paid readings will follow — the Everyday Reading at $14 for a further seven minutes, and the Full Reading at $29, which adds the Personality, EI and Closeness Mirrors and reads the whole thing together rather than reporting it separately.
landing.price_ceiling: $29 is the ceiling for the whole practice. The promise page commits us to publishing a maximum before anything is purchasable, and that is it.
landing.nothing_built_yet: Neither is built yet. They are described here so you can see what is coming and what it will cost. Nothing on this page takes a card, and nothing renews.
landing.thinking_body: These instruments came out of a book — Relationship Tracks — which makes the argument at length, using railway signalling as a way of thinking about how people choose and why they stay. It isn't published yet.
landing.thinking_essays: Five essays drawn from it are free to read, and they will tell you inside a paragraph whether this is for you.

samples.sten_explainer: Sten scores run 1–10. We show your position, not a verdict: establishing the reference sample that would make ‘high’ or ‘low’ mean something is work we have not finished, and until it is we don't say it.
samples.loudest_line: The full result names the factors sitting furthest from your own middle, in either direction — the ones doing most of the selecting.
samples.personality_note: The full result scores fifteen primary factors and five global dimensions, with validity checks.

methodology_note._note: Published version of docs/METHODOLOGY_NOTE_DRAFT.md, approved verbatim. Hash-locked because these are the paragraphs most likely to be softened later: the fourth admits we could not establish a reference population, the fifth says we removed the claims rather than caveating them, the sixth discloses that the naming threshold is provisional rather than derived, and the seventh accounts for the readings already delivered under the old language. Deliberately contains no figures, does not name the parent product, and does not mention the reliability gates.
methodology_note.heading: What our numbers rest on
methodology_note.lead: Every instrument here reports a number. This is where each of those numbers comes from, including the two places where the honest answer is “not from as much as you'd want”.
methodology_note.established: The Personality Mirror and the EI Mirror are established instruments. Five-factor structure and a four-domain emotional intelligence model are among the most replicated findings in the field. That is a statement about the constructs, not about our arithmetic, and the two are worth keeping apart.
methodology_note.developmental: Our own instruments are developmental and labelled as such. The Essential, Closeness and Everyday Mirrors use questions we wrote. Their properties are still being established. The Everyday Mirror has not yet been tested for whether one option in each pair sounds more flattering than the other, which is a real gap and stated on the instrument itself.
methodology_note.stopped_comparing: We have stopped comparing you with other people. Until recently, a personality factor was reported as how many people sit further toward one end than you, and each factor carried a band word — very high, average, very low. Both of those are claims about a population. When we went looking for the population, we could not establish one: the score bands we inherited record no sample size, no group and no date, all fifteen factors share the same generic lower cut-offs, and the band widths look like an even split of the possible range rather than a map of how people actually score.
methodology_note.removed_not_caveated: So we removed those statements rather than printing a caveat beside them. A footnote admitting the comparison rests on nothing, under a sentence making the comparison anyway, is worse than either on its own.
methodology_note.what_is_left: What is left is everything that never needed a population: which way you lean on each factor, and which three sit furthest from your own middle. Those are facts about your answers.
methodology_note.still_rests_on: What that still rests on. Naming your three furthest requires knowing how much of the distance is signal and how much is measurement noise, and we have not measured that for these item banks either. The threshold we use — a factor has to sit a stated distance from your own average before we name it — is a deliberately conservative provisional choice, not a figure derived from our own data. When we have measured it, that number will change, and we will say so here first.
methodology_note.already_delivered: Readings delivered before this change carry the older comparative language. We have not altered them, because a delivered reading is a record of what we said at the time rather than a live document. This page is the account of what changed and why.
methodology_note.if_ever: If a reference sample is ever built, we will publish how many people are in it and who they are before any comparison appears in a reading.
